text: What if my roommate knew about contemporary Nigerian music. <break time="0.8s" /> Talented people singing in English and Pidgin, and Igbo and Yoruba and Ijo, mixing influences from Jay Z to Fela to Bob Marley to their grandfathers. <break time="0.8s" /> What if my roommate knew about the female lawyer who recently went to court in Nigeria to challenge a ridiculous law that required women to get their husbands consent before renewing their passports. <break time="0.8s" /> What if my roommate knew about Nollywood, full of innovative people making films despite great technical odds. <break time="0.8s" /> Films so popular that they really are the best example of Nigerians consuming what they produce. <break time="0.8s" /> What if my roommate knew about my wonderfully ambitious hair braider, who has just started her own business selling hair extensions. <break time="0.8s" /> Or about the millions of other Nigerians who start businesses and sometimes fail, but continue to nurse ambition. <break time="0.8s" /> Every time I am home I am confronted with the usual sources of irritation for most Nigerians, our failed infrastructure, our failed government. <break time="0.8s" /> But also by the incredible resilience of people who thrive despite the government, rather than because of it. <break time="0.8s" /> I teach writing workshops in Lagos every summer. <break time="0.8s" /> And it is amazing to me how many people apply, how many people are eager to write, to tell stories. <break time="0.8s" /> My Nigerian publisher and I have just started a non profit called Farafina Trust. <break time="0.8s" /> And we have big dreams of building libraries and refurbishing libraries that already exist, and providing books for state schools that do not have anything in their libraries, and also of organizing lots and lots of workshops, in reading and writing, for all the people who are eager to tell our many stories. <break time="0.8s" /> Stories matter. <break time="0.8s" /> Many stories matter. <break time="0.8s" /> Stories have been used to dispossess and to malign. <break time="0.8s" /> But stories can also be used to empower, and to humanize. <break time="0.8s" /> Stories can break the dignity of a people. <break time="0.8s" /> But stories can also repair that broken dignity. <break time="0.8s" /> The American writer Alice Walker wrote this about her southern relatives who had moved to the north. <break time="0.8s" /> She introduced them to a book about the southern life that they had left behind, They sat around, reading the book themselves, listening to me read the book, and a kind of paradise was regained. <break time="0.8s" /> I would like to end with this thought, that when we reject the single story, when we realize that there is never a single story about any place, we regain a kind of paradise.
